sections.body: Regulatory change mapping is the practice of tracking new and amended AI laws, rules, guidance, enforcement actions, and standards across jurisdictions, then linking each change to specific obligations, controls, owners, and deadlines inside an organization. It covers horizontal regimes such as privacy, consumer protection, employment, and intellectual property, as well as sector rules for health, finance, and education. For AI specifically, it also covers model transparency, data provenance, bias testing, and incident reporting duties. The field sits in corporate governance and regulatory compliance, where the output is a defensible map from external text to internal policy and evidence.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: It runs on a maintained source register, legal databases, official gazettes, regulator feeds, legislative tracking services, and internal policy repositories. Teams often use spreadsheets, GRC platforms, and document management systems, with version control and audit logs. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages and 6947 state AI bills illustrate the volume of source material that such a system must ingest and classify. Mapping tools may include citation graphs, obligation libraries, and control frameworks, but the core infrastructure is structured text, metadata, and review workflow.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts monitor sources, capture the change, summarize it, and assign a jurisdiction, topic, and effective date. They then map each provision to internal obligations, controls, policies, and risk owners, often using a crosswalk or traceability matrix. Reviewers validate the mapping with legal, compliance, and business stakeholders, and the map is updated when guidance or enforcement shifts. For AI, the method also tracks case law and enforcement patterns, such as the site's 29 AI case law precedents and 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, to show how regulators and courts are interpreting existing rules.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because every mapped obligation should trace back to a primary source, with a citation, retrieval date, and version history. Rights and risk include licensing limits on republishing legal text, confidentiality of internal controls, and the risk of acting on an outdated or misread provision. Access controls, review sign off, and change logs help show who changed what and why. The map should distinguish binding law from guidance, draft bills, and commentary, and it should flag uncertainty rather than present all sources as equally authoritative.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Regulatory change mapping is moving toward more continuous monitoring, structured obligation data, and machine assisted classification, while keeping human review for interpretation and judgment. Expect closer links between regulatory maps and AI governance registers, model cards, impact assessments, and incident logs. As AI bills and lawsuits multiply, the map will need to cover overlapping state, federal, and international requirements and to show conflicts and gaps. The practical goal is a living record that helps an organization see what changed, what it means for its controls, and what evidence it can produce.
